topic: PhoneBuddy: Embedded Rust LLM Agent Engine for Mobile
summary: PhoneBuddy SDK (APUS-AI-Lab/PhoneBuddySDK) is an Apache-2.0, pure-Rust agent harness you embed directly inside an iOS or Android app. Its whole pitch is that it removes the desktop-agent assumption App stores forbid — no fork/exec, no std::process::Command, no tokio::process — and replaces it with in-process equivalents: a ReAct tool loop, an in-memory BusyBox-style virtual shell, a jailed file sandbox, a boa_engine JavaScript sandbox, in-memory subagents, cron-style scheduled tasks and human-in-the-loop callbacks, all behind a C ABI with Swift and Kotlin wrappers. It is derived from xAI's grok-build harness (NOTICE lists the modifications). Independent verification on 2026-10-01 holds up on the central static claim: a full source download of main (commit c2fc7ea, 2026-09-13) contains 70 .rs files and ZERO occurrences of std::process::Command or tokio::process, and no fork/exec/posix_spawn. The weak points are unchanged from the September audit: no public CI (.github absent), one unanswered MCP/Agent-Skills roadmap issue, no local model inference path, and a README that still asserts it 'passes Apple App Store and Google Play sandbox reviews' with no public review record. VERDICT: credible architecture, thin verification and adoption (36 stars, 3 releases, latest v0.2.0).

Early 2026 enforcement wave: Replit, Vibecode and similar build-on-phone tools blocked from updates under 2.5.2
Allowed: JavaScript in JavaScriptCore/WKWebView (no change to primary purpose), WebKit content, server-driven config/feature flags
Not allowed: downloading native code, runtime code generation (dlopen, JSC eval for new features), building/installing standalone apps in-app, plugin systems adding post-review functionality
DPCLA 3.3.2 is the actual escape hatch for interpreted code — and it is restricted to built-in WebKit/JavaScriptCore

Apple Guideline 2.5.2 (verified verbatim 2026-10-01): 'Apps should be self-contained in their bundles, and may not read or write data outside the designated container area, nor may they download, install, or execute code which introduces or changes features or functionality of the app' — with a narrow educational-code exception

Google Play Device and Network Abuse (verified verbatim 2026-10-01): 'an app may not download executable code (such as dex, JAR, .so files) from a source other than Google Play. This restriction does not apply to code that runs in a virtual machine or an interpreter where either provides indirect access to Android APIs (such as JavaScript in a webview or browser)' — the interpreter carve-out that keeps an embedded JS engine viable

Same Play policy adds: interpreted-language code 'loaded at run time (for example, not packaged with the app) must not allow potential violations of Google Play policies' — the compliance burden lands on the host app

Apple Developer Program License Agreement 3.3.2 permits interpreted code 'run by the built-in WebKit framework or JavaScriptCore', provided scripts do not change the app's primary purpose — this is what an embedded non-WebKit engine must be argued against
Early-2026 App Store enforcement blocked update releases for Replit, Vibecode and similar vibe-coding apps under 2.5.2

Independent audit found PhoneBuddySDK has static controls for file boundaries, SSRF screening, tool timeouts, script loop limits, repeated-tool detection, cancellation, and Swift/Kotlin/C integration — but 'no public App Store or Google Play review record was found' and the passed-review claim 'remains a project assertion'
Audit also disputes 'guaranteed FFI panic containment' as an unsupported claim — relevant because the C ABI is the mobile integration surface

A separate research project also named PhoneBuddy (PhoneBuddyAI/phonebuddy) reports 83.2% AndroidWorld success and 45.33% on a 150-task real-phone human eval by combining real-app RL with mock-app (PhoneWorld) training; it has 61 stars and an unrelated scope

Apple Foundation Models framework (iOS 26) exposes the ~3B on-device model on the Neural Engine with no download and no API key; Gemini Nano ships via AICore on Android flagships with an allow-listed device set

On-device runtime landscape is crowded and mature where PhoneBuddy is thin: llama.rn 1,047 stars (MIT, pushed 2026-10-01), LiteRT-LM 6,549, Cactus 6,081, Cactus Needle 12,899, mlc-llm 23,202, MNN 16,159, ncnn 23,905
MCP's stdio transport assumes a local process on the same machine, which fails on mobile; Streamable HTTP is now the recommended transport for remote MCP, and mobile client SDKs (Swift/Kotlin) exist

PhoneBuddy README claims 'Passes Apple App Store and Google Play app sandbox security reviews with zero permission escalations' — no artifact, review record or CI run was found to support it (repo has no .github, no review docs)

README advertises 1:1 network emulation of desktop AI coding clients (xAI grok-build, OpenAI Codex, Anthropic Claude Code) including User-Agent and wire-schema mimicry — a distinctive and legally/spiritually questionable feature for a mobile SDK

A 'PhoneBuddy' HN story ('Google banned our mobile AI agent app for doing what Gemini should do, but doesnt', 2026-04-02) drew 4 points and 1 comment, where a mobile-security dev describes Accessibility-API abuse as the top mobile-agent headache — context for why the in-process, no-Accessibility design matters

angles: The one-line thesis: App Review Guideline 2.5.2 turns 'spawn a shell' into an architectural prohibition, and PhoneBuddy is the first Rust harness built around that prohibition instead of around Linux.

Show the exact forbidden primitives and their in-process replacements, with counts: 0 std::process::Command, 0 tokio::process, 0 fork/exec — versus a BusyBox-style virtual shell, boa_engine JS, jailed file tools.

The honest 2.5.2 reading: 2.5.2 is about downloading/executing code that changes functionality, not about forking per se. DPCLA 3.3.2 blesses interpreted code only inside WebKit/JavaScriptCore. So an embedded non-WebKit engine must be argued, not assumed — this is the sharpest compliance point in the article.

The Play side is friendlier and quotable: the interpreter/VM carve-out explicitly permits JS-in-interpreter, with the caveat that runtime-loaded interpreted code must not enable policy violations. Quote it verbatim.
The passed-review claim is a claim. Contrast the README assertion with the audit's finding that no public review record exists and no CI exists.

Name-collision disambiguation is genuinely useful to readers: 'PhoneBuddy' now means two things (an embeddable Rust SDK vs a phone-use training/model line with an arXiv paper and HuggingFace weights). Explaining which one you are evaluating is a differentiator no competitor article has.

The missing piece nobody advertises: PhoneBuddy has no model. It is a harness. On a modern phone you pair it with Apple Foundation Models (iOS) or Gemini Nano/LiteRT-LM (Android) or a GGUF via llama.rn. Frame the SDK as the agent layer, not an inference stack.

MCP is the elephant: the mobile MCP problem is real (stdio assumes a local process), mobile MCP patterns exist, and PhoneBuddy's only open issue is asking for MCP/Agent Skills support with zero replies. That gap is the article's forward-looking section.

'Derived from grok-build' cuts both ways: it inherits a battle-tested agent loop and 27k-star upstream credibility, but a mobile app embedding it also inherits desktop-shaped assumptions (context budget, TUI-era tool names) and a NOTICE obligation.

The 1:1 desktop-client impersonation feature (fake User-Agent for Grok Build / Codex / Claude Code) is a distinctive angle — useful for compatibility, awkward for a commercial mobile app's terms-of-service posture.

Adoption reality check: 36 stars, 13 forks, 1 open issue, 3 releases, HEAD quiet since 2026-09-13. Compare with the runtime neighbours it depends on (llama.rn 1k stars, LiteRT-LM 6.5k) to show it is an early bet, not infrastructure.

Security framing: an in-process agent that can read/write a jailed directory and run bounded JS is attack surface inside your app. The audit's static evidence (path jailing, SSRF block on loopback/private ranges, script loop limits, cancellation) is the thing to verify, and 'guaranteed panic containment' across the C boundary is explicitly not proven.

faq.q: Is PhoneBuddy SDK free to use commercially?
faq.a: Yes — it is Apache-2.0, so it can be embedded in proprietary apps with attribution (the repo ships a NOTICE crediting grok-build). This is the decisive licensing advantage over Ant Group's Napaxi, which is GPL-3.0.

faq.q: Does PhoneBuddy run an LLM on the phone?
faq.a: No. PhoneBuddy is the agent harness — planning, tools, sandbox, subagents. Inference is host-supplied: you pair it with Apple Foundation Models on iOS, Gemini Nano/LiteRT-LM on Android, or a GGUF via llama.rn, or with a cloud provider.

faq.q: Does it really pass App Store and Google Play review?
faq.a: Unverified. The README asserts it does; no public review record, CI run, or third-party attestation was found on 2026-10-01. Treat it as a project claim and run your own 2.5.2/DPCLA 3.3.2 analysis.

faq.q: Does it spawn processes or use fork/exec?
faq.a: Verified no. A full source download of main (c2fc7ea) contains zero std::process::Command, zero tokio::process, and no fork/exec/posix_spawn references across 70 Rust files.

faq.q: Is the embedded JavaScript engine allowed by the app stores?
faq.a: Google Play's Device and Network Abuse policy carves out code run in an interpreter or VM that provides indirect Android API access, so an embedded JS engine is viable there. Apple's 2.5.2 is stricter: DPCLA 3.3.2 blesses interpreted code only via built-in WebKit/JavaScriptCore, so a non-WebKit engine is an argument you have to make.

faq.q: Is PhoneBuddy the same as the PhoneBuddy paper with PhoneBuddy-4B models?
faq.a: No. That is an unrelated research line (PhoneBuddyAI/phonebuddy, arXiv 2606.23049) about training phone-use models with real-app plus mock-app RL. The SDK reviewed here is APUS-AI-Lab/PhoneBuddySDK.

faq.q: Does PhoneBuddy support MCP or Agent Skills?
faq.a: Not yet. The repo's only open issue (opened 2026-09-11) asks about a roadmap for MCP and Agent Skills and has no answer; the engine exposes its own tool set and a host-routing LLM layer instead.

It had three releases in five days in August 2026 (v0.1.1, v0.1.2, v0.2.0), then main went quiet: HEAD is 2026-09-13, with no commits in the 2.5 weeks before 2026-10-01. Early, small, but not abandoned as of this writing.
